newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hails arrests in Samper drug case.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hails arrests in Samper drug case.

text.p: The U.S. State Department on Monday hailed the arrest of 11 Colombian Air Force personnel in connection with the discovery of heroin stashed on President Ernesto Samper's official jet, and said it did not intend to take any action in the matter.
"Our understanding is that Colombian law enforcement officials are taking the right kinds of steps to deal with this criminal act," deputy spokesman Glynn Davies told reporters.

"I don't think that there's any action that we (the United States) need to take since the Colombians seem to be pursuing this vigorously and well, and they've, as I say, made some arrests, so that's a good sign," he added.
As Samper left for New York on Saturday to address the U.N. General Assembly, he was caught in a new drug scandal over heroin found stashed on his presidential jet.
The embarrassing discovery on board the presidential Boeing 707 was made at the Catam military air base near Bogota during an inspection prompted by an anonymous telephone caller.

Police and military officials said 7.4 pounds (3.4 kg) of heroin were found hidden in 14 small packets stashed in the nose and tail section of the aircraft at the air base where the jet was being readied for the flight to New York.
The plane is owned and operated by the Colombian Air Force, and National Police chief Gen. Rosso Jose Serrano has said air force personnel were among prime suspects.
Military and judicial officials said on Sunday that an air force colonel, a major, several captains and a sergeant were among the 11 people who had been arrested for questioning in the scandal.
The 11 were all involved in a test flight of the 707 on Friday in which it flew from Bogota to the southwest city of Cali and then on to the northwest city of Medellin before returning to Catam.
Davies asserted the detention of suspects shows that it is a lie that "somehow forces outside of Colombia were responsible for planting these drugs."
That "clearly is not the case, because some people have already been picked up in Colombia and their investigation's proceeding," he said.
Samper, in a speech to the General Assembly on Monday, cast his nation as that of a victim and proposed setting up a "grand alliance" to fight the scourge of drugs.
"Colombia wants to be part of the solution," Samper said. "We do not want to continue to be demonized when, in fact, we are all victims."

The U.S. State Department spokesman said Washington was glad the heroin was discovered before the plane landed in New York. "We're glad the drugs were found before they hit the streets in the United States and added to the drug problem here in this country," he said.
While the arrests are good news, many questions remain, including why the drugs were hidden in the plane and whether the aim was to make a profit or a political point, he said.

Samper, who has defied repeated calls for his resignation because of charges his 1994 election campaign was partly financed by the Cali drug cartel, told reporters before his departure from Colombia that the latest incident was the work of someone seeking to hurt him.

Samper's U.S. visa was revoked in July because of his alleged ties to drug traffickers and as a sign of Washington's displeasure over a move by Colombia's Congress to clear him of drug corruption charges a month earlier. The travel restriction does not apply to heads of state visiting the U.N. headquarters.
